era: medieval Bengal and the mythic geography of the Manasamangal
target_audience: readers of Bengali mythology, devotional poetry, women's narratives, and contemporary Indian philosophical verse
book_summary: Behula: The River of Devotion is a poetry sequence in which Behula, the heroine of the Manasamangal, speaks as bride, widow, pilgrim, and defiant lover. The book begins on her wedding night, when her husband Lakhindar is bitten by a serpent and dies, and follows her refusal of the widow's silence. She builds a raft, lays her husband's body upon it, and sails the river for months, enduring storms, hunger, and the mockery of the world, until she reaches the court of the gods. There her devotion moves Lord Indra himself, who grants Lakhindar his life back, while the bhat flower of the riverbank weeps upon her foot in witness to her sacrifice. The poems do not treat devotion as passive endurance; they treat it as an active argument with fate, a woman's love strong enough to move heaven. By the end, Behula does not boast of her triumph. She asks what devotion is worth when it is not witnessed, and what a society owes to a woman who refuses to be buried with her husband.
gist: Behula, the Bengali heroine of the Manasamangal, sacrifices her social life and braves the river of death to revive her dead husband Lakhindar, her devotion so great that Lord Indra himself honours her character and the bhat flower weeps upon her foot.

chapters.chapter_summary: The serpent's shadow falls across the wedding chamber, and a bride's world ends in a single night. The context draws on the epic's opening wound: love struck down before it could begin.
Society arrives with its rituals and its pity, expecting a woman to be buried alive in mourning. The context turns on the refusal of that silence and the first stirring of defiance.
A funeral becomes a voyage as a woman lays her husband's body on a raft and steers it down the river. The context holds the image of a corpse carried as if it were a living passenger.
Storms, hunger, and the loneliness of the water mark the long voyage. The context follows the river as both enemy and road, the threshold between the living and the dead.
People on the banks call her mad, a woman chasing a dead man. The context turns on her answer: that love is not measured by what the world can see.
A mortal woman pleads her case before the gods, and her devotion is weighed against divine decree. The context holds the moment a human love is finally heard in heaven.
Lord Indra, moved by her character, grants Lakhindar his life back. The context turns on the recognition that her sacrifice was for love, not reward, and yet heaven itself bowed.
The humble flower of the riverbank is said to have wept upon her foot. The context holds the image of the earth itself crying in witness to her devotion.
She returns with her husband restored, but she is no longer the sheltered bride who left. The context turns on what the journey has made of her.

The concluding poem gathers the wedding night, the raft, the river, the mockery, the court, and the weeping flower into one final address. The context asks what devotion is worth when it is not witnessed.
The days in the ward become a single long night, and waiting becomes its own labour. The context turns on the thousand small acts of staying that no one sees.
The medicine has a price not written on the bottle, and she pays it coin by coin without paying with her soul. The context turns on the refusal to be bought.
When the blood banks run empty, she gives what runs in her own veins. The context turns on the small, bodily gift of the self that no one can take.
The city closes itself against the sickness, and she defies the checkpoints to reach the hospital every day. The context turns on a love that obeys a higher law.
The doctor brings the words she had stopped daring to hope for, and the long road ends in a return. The context turns on the benediction of a love that was answered.
